title: The theater experience isn't my favorite anymore...[Poor Things Spoilers]

commenti.body:
If you want a better understanding of Poor Things,[then this will help](https://filmcolossus.com/poor-things-2023-explained). 

It’s a bit deeper than you’re giving it credit for. But also isn’t all that deep.

I think there are a few issues with this idea.

The first, and biggest problem to me, is this idea that films are supposed to be clearly trying to say something. Few films are really that clear about what they’re saying, and those few that are are rarely deeper than a superficial moral. It’s not a didactic or fable based or parabalistic genre for the most part. Honestly even the best films with explicit messages rarely get deeper than “capitalism is bad” or something.

This isn’t just the nature of movies, but of art. A “clear point” only really exists when there is a simple message like the one you stated. Most movies and most art is meant to make you think, ask more questions than it answers, etc.

Ignoring this, every word of dialogue is not important. Firstly because film is a visual medium. A great film will often be fairly easy to follow without sound at all. It is a visual medium. Moreover, anything that is that important to the plot or theme or “message” of a movie will be stated over and over and over. Film is not an exceedingly subtle medium even in its most challenging and complex forms. And again, in all art, themes are woven throughout. If it’s only stated once, or even twice or thrice, then that’s not the message or theme or core idea of the piece of art, that’s just a line with an interesting idea.

Also I’d really try not to rewind films, personally. I think that focusing on little details and missed things will actually make it harder to catch the bigger idea. You need to take a step back to see those big things, not a step closer. 

It’s cool if the themes in Poor Things didn’t vibe with you. It is not a movie with a clear point most challenging films aren’t. I would venture that you would have to miss a good amount of words in the film to miss its themes. There aren’t any words quite so precious that you’re missing a whole clear point. 

Just a tiny side point, maybe find one with better surround sound? A Dolby one or something? Or wait until the last week of its run where they do daytime showings with subtitles in theatres? I’m unable to hear whispering in modern films without subtitles at home, so I feel ya, but I’ve personally never had this problem in theatres, I’d try to find one with a better speaker system.

I'd argue that not every word is important, but you can get listening assistive devices for most films, or find showings with subtitles. You can still do closed captions at most films.

I saw Dream scenario and Nightmare Alley in the theaters with subtitles.
I also feel like the movie isn’t trying to be super deep. I feel like people want it to be something it isn’t.

Hard disagree. If you are not picking up on themes/dialogue/etc, it’s best to try and watch the film again. Most films are not meant to be understood on a single watch (unless they’re explicitly “entertainment”). Give yourself to reflect on what you DID gather from the film, what you did/did not like, then go back and see what you noticed differently.

And as much as I’ve been guilty of turning on subtitles/rewinding at home… they do mess with your appreciation of any given film. I think this is a common but terrible side effect of home viewing - you’re focusing your attention on dialogue when it can or should be directed elsewhere, you’re interrupting the rhythm of the storytelling, etc. 

Challenging films are exactly meant to be that… don’t be so hard on yourself, and also give yourself a chance to engage in that challenge rather than finding external tools to ease it.
My local Cinemark has subtitles on screen for matinees on Saturday and Monday. The listings say (OC) after the title or on-screen caption in the description.

You have trained yourself to have a difficult time understanding dialogue by using subtitles at home. I went cold turkey on no longer using subtitles because I realized I spent the entire time reading and missing emotion on the faces of the characters and other things like cinematography of each scene. After a few months I realized how much better I was picking up the dialogue and how much of a crutch the subtitles were and how it had essentially made my ears lazy for lack of a better word.
